A content delivery network solves a simple problem: the computer that originally stores a website, called the origin server, might sit far away, making pages load slowly for distant visitors. To fix this, copies of that content get placed on many servers scattered around the world, known as edge locations, positioned closer to where people actually are. When someone requests a page and a nearby edge location already holds a saved copy, that's called a cache hit — the request gets answered instantly without ever bothering the distant origin server. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries stocking popular books so nobody has to travel to one central library across the country every time they want to read something. If a particular edge location doesn't have the requested content saved yet, it quietly fetches it from the origin server once, stores it, and serves it faster to everyone nearby afterward. This system reduces waiting time, spreads out traffic so no single server gets overwhelmed, and keeps things running even if one location has trouble, since others can pick up the load. Streaming video, loading a news article, or checking a store's inventory all become quicker because of this behind-the-scenes network of copies working together.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing the real, master copy of a website's content | Everything ultimately starts here, so protecting it from too much direct traffic keeps things stable |
| Edge location | A server positioned near a group of visitors instead of far away | Being physically closer means less travel time, so pages appear faster |
| Cache hit | A moment when saved content nearby is used instead of fetching it from afar | More cache hits mean quicker loading and less strain on the original source |
| Cache miss | A moment when nearby storage lacks the content, so it's fetched from origin | Explains why the very first request for something can feel slower than later ones |
